title: Microenvironmental barriers to healing in osteoradionecrosis and opportunities for regenerative intervention

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Microenvironmental barriers to healing in osteoradionecrosis and opportunities for regenerative intervention》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0035】Global cancer incidence is projected to rise to 28.4 million cases by 2040, representing a 47% increase from 2020, with a disproportionately higher burden in transitioning countries [1]. Among these malignancies, head and neck cancer (HNC), the seventh most common cancer worldwide, remains a major contributor, accounting for approximately 940,000 new cases and 480,000 deaths annually worldwide, according to the Global Cancer Observatory estimates for 2022 [[2], [3], [4]]. Over 90% of HNCs are squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC) arising from the mucosal linings of the oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, or hypopharynx, with additional cases originating from cutaneous squamous cells. Less commonly, HNCs also present as adenocarcinomas of salivary or head and neck glands. These malignancies exhibit substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity driven by anatomical location and tumor origin [5].

【Introduction · p0040】Management of HNC is guided by tumor- and patient-related factors, with treatment typically involving surgery, radiotherapy (RT), and/or systemic therapy including chemotherapy, targeted agents, or immunotherapy, delivered as single or combined modalities depending on disease stage and location [6]. RT plays a central role in HNC management and is used in approximately 75% of patients with HNSCC, either as a primary treatment or as adjuvant therapy following surgical resection, due to its efficacy in achieving local tumor control in early-stage disease [[7], [8], [9]].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Microenvironmental barriers to healing in osteoradionecrosis and opportunities for regenerative intervention》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Biomaterial- and scaffold-based regenerative strategies · p0315】A wide range of bone grafting and reconstructive techniques have been used to restore mandibular defects [[151], [152], [153], [154]]; however, many of these approaches are limited by donor-site morbidity, high cost, and the low availability of the autogenous graft material, which remains the clinical gold standard [155,156]. These limitations are further compounded in ORN, where radiation-induced hypovascularity, fibrosis, and cellular dysfunction weaken graft integration and healing [90]. Consequently, there has been sustained interest in the development of tissue-engineered alternatives that employ synthetic and biologically active materials to promote bone regeneration in irradiated tissue [157]. In this context, natural and synthetic composite scaffolds, ceramic biomaterials, osteogenic and angiogenic growth factors, and stem cell therapies are increasingly being integrated into combination strategies to support the healing of irradiated bone tissue (Table 3) [135,35,36,158,159]. Thus, as the field of tissue engineering evolves, inert bone substitute materials that have been historically used as passive space holders during the healing process are now insufficient on their own to drive true regeneration [160].

【Scaffold design principles and osteoconductive strategies · p0320】Scaffolds serve as engineered 3D constructs that are designed to mimic features of the ECM to support cell attachment, tissue ingrowth, and bone regeneration. Through defined pore size and interconnectivity, scaffolds regulate cell adhesion, migration, and osteogenic differentiation while facilitating vascular infiltration and oxygen diffusion [168]. With scaffolds, characteristics such as surface chemistry and ligand presentation govern adhesion and integrin signaling; stiffness, viscoelasticity, and architecture influence mechano-transduction and lineage commitment; pore interconnectivity and degradation regulate vascular invasion and tissue remodeling; and affinity, mesh size, or responsive chemistries determine therapeutic retention and release [169]. In irradiated bone, these design variables must additionally be judged by whether they preserve cell survival, restore osteogenic-angiogenic coupling, normalize inflammatory and oxidative states, and remain functional within fibrotic, hypoxic, and poorly vascularized tissue. Scaffolds may be fabricated as hydrogels, cryogels, nanofibrous matrices, particulate systems, ceramics, or 3D-printed constructs and may incorporate natural polymers, synthetic polymers, calcium-phosphate bioceramics, or composite combinations [170]. These material classes offer different advantages in cell interaction, mechanics, and degradation for osteogenic regeneration.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Microenvironmental barriers to healing in osteoradionecrosis and opportunities for regenerative intervention》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · p0520】ORN should no longer be seen solely as an inexorable consequence of structural tissue destruction, but rather as a pathological state perpetuated by a maladaptive irradiated microenvironment. This conceptual shift reframes treatment from the mere replacement of necrotic tissue toward the restoration of regenerative competence. The integration of senescence-targeted interventions with biomaterial, cellular, and molecular regenerative platforms may therefore represent the most cogent path toward durable recovery by concurrently dismantling the biological impediments to healing and reinstating the mechanisms required for functional bone regeneration.

【Osteoblasts and osteoprogenitors · p0115】Damage to osteoblasts and their progenitors is a primary contributor to reduced bone mineral density following irradiation [[51], [52], [53]]. Radiation reduces osteoblast number and matrix formation, and both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate impaired osteoblast proliferation and differentiation, cell-cycle arrest, decreased collagen production, and increased sensitivity to apoptotic stimuli [51,54]. Because of their short lifespan, continual repopulation of osteoblasts through osteogenic differentiation of MSCs is essential. However, in irradiated tissue, MSC numbers, clonogenicity, and osteogenic differentiation capacity are reduced, delaying recovery of functional osteoblast populations [55]. Radiation also promotes a shift of MSC fate toward adipogenesis at the expense of osteogenesis, contributing to marrow adiposity and further suppression of bone formation. Oxidative stress contributes significantly to early osteoprogenitor damage and persistent lineage dysfunction [56].

(A) Hierarchical organization of bone, including compact and cancellous bone, osteons, trabeculae, and major bone cell types. (B) Immediate and late effects of radiation on the bone microenvironment. (C) Major inducers and hallmarks of cellular senescence. (A) Reproduced with permission from Ref. [42]. (B) Reproduced from Ref. [43] under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. (C) Reproduced from Ref. 【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 Mechanism of MSC-based therapy in ORN. MSCs may support regeneration within the irradiated bone microenvironment through (1) paracrine secretion of angiogenic and osteogenic factors such as VEGF, FGF, cytokines, and extracellular vesicles; (2) cell-surface protein and chemokine-mediated signaling that promotes intercellular communication, cell migration, and recruitment of reparative populations; (3) immunomodulation that shifts macrophages from a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype (reduced IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6) toward an M2 phenotype (increased IL-10 and TGF-β), reduces T cell activation and effector cytokine production, and limits dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation, thereby attenuating persistent inflammatory signaling; and (4) protection against radiation-associated cellular stress, including regulation of oxidative stress and iron homeostasis. Created in BioRender. Hixon, K. (2026) https://BioRender.com/p0lgo8r.

【Fig. 3 · fig3】Fig. 3 Stem cell- and EV-focused approaches for ORN. (A) Three-dimensional (3D) microCT images of irradiated rat extraction sockets: (i) Matrigel-4, (ii) tonsil-derived MSC-4, (iii) Matrigel-1, and (iv) tonsil-derived MSC-1 groups. Complete bone regeneration was observed in the tonsil-derived MSC-1 group. (B) Effects of human dental pulp stem cell-derived small EVs in a rat model: (i) RT-PCR analysis of senescence-associated mRNA expression; (ii) representative mandibular specimens, with black arrowheads indicating extraction sites; and (iii) representative hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained mandibular sections, with black arrowheads indicating enlarged extraction sites. Scale bar: 1 mm. (C) (i) Western blot and (ii) quantitative analyses of AKT and phosphorylated AKT expression in BMSCs under control, 12-Gy irradiation, and 12-Gy irradiation plus human amniotic MSC-derived small EV treatment. (D) Effects of CYR61-associated migrasomes on irradiated BMSCs: (i) Transwell migration quantification and western blots of ALP, RUNX2, and OSX; (ii) quantification of ALP, RUNX2, and OSX protein expression.
